implementation_notes: Modern C++ ships the synchronization primitives but no bounded blocking queue, so the classic structure is a template class over std::deque (or a fixed ring) guarded by std::mutex, with two std::condition_variable instances for not_empty/not_full; push waits through the predicated overload (wait(lock, [&]{ return size < cap; })), which already loops against spurious wakeups. Waiting methods need std::unique_lock; the full-queue policy (block, wait_for with timeout, try_push returning false) is part of the interface. When a bounded queue already exists in the stack (Boost.Asio/executor queues, oneTBB concurrent_bounded_queue, moodycamel), use it instead of writing a second one.
pitfalls: A bare cv.wait(lk) without the predicate reintroduces spurious-wakeup and lost-wakeup bugs; always use wait(lock, pred) or a while loop.
One condition variable for both empty and full waiters lets a consumer steal a producer's wakeup; use two condition variables (or notify_all) so each waiter class is woken for its own reason.
Notifying while holding the lock is legal but wakes a thread that immediately blocks on the mutex; unlock first (or notify at scope exit) for throughput.
std::condition_variable only works with std::unique_lock<std::mutex>; lock_guard in a waiting method does not compile, and condition_variable_any is needed for other lock types.

variants.name: C++20 counting semaphores over a ring buffer (Dijkstra form)
variants.idiom_name: std::counting_semaphore empty/full slots + atomic ring indices
variants.implementation_notes: C++20's std::counting_semaphore makes Dijkstra's original two-semaphore solution directly expressible: one semaphore counts empty slots (initialized to the capacity) and one counts filled slots (initialized to zero), the ring indices are atomics, and acquire()/release() replace the condition variables and the predicate loop entirely. Semaphores are not tied to threads, so acquiring in one thread and releasing in another is exactly the intended producer/consumer hand-off; try_acquire_for gives a bounded wait, and the standard warns that try_acquire can fail spuriously, so a failed try means 'not yet' and never an error. Choose it when the toolchain is C++20 and the lock-free hand-off or the simpler code path matters.
pitfalls: try_acquire may fail spuriously by specification; a retry loop must treat that as 'not ready', not as a failure to report.
The semaphore counts must match the capacity exactly (empty_ = capacity, full_ = 0); an off-by-one silently becomes a data race or a permanent stall.
An exception or early return between acquire and release leaks a slot forever; guard the critical step so release always runs.
